secrets: father died owing the Ziani forty ducats

persona.backstory: Son of a rope-maker who died in the fever of 1340, leaving a hank of unpaid debt and a bench in the Arsenale. Marco walks to work along the fondamenta before dawn, keeps his mother Agnese fed, and counts the ducats it would take to put his own name over a warehouse door at the Rialto.

conversations.says: Eat, you look thin.

Caterina, I am at the rope bench before dawn every day. When I have something to offer, I will not come to you empty-handed.

Maria, I mean to have my name over a door on this bridge one day. Remember it: Dandolo.

talk.say: Alvise — we share a name. I am Marco, son of Zuane the rope-maker of Castello, dead this spring. I know rope, rigging and greek, and I can count. When your bench needs a young man who will not steal from you, remember there is a Dandolo at the Arsenale.
Ser Gritti, Marco Dandolo. If ever you want cordage for a hull judged by a man who made it, come to me at the Arsenale and I will tell you true whether it is sound.
Mother, we eat plain but we eat. Keep the door shut to anyone claiming father's paper — send them to me.

talk.say: Caterina, I will not pretend to be richer than I am. I have a bench at the Arsenale, a mother to keep, and my father's debt of forty on my back. But I am twenty-two, I do not drink my wages, and I mean to have my name over a warehouse door at the Rialto before I am forty. Marry me and everything I build is yours and our children's. I promise you honesty about money — always.
Mother, I am courting Caterina. Speak well of me to her. I want children in this house while you are still here to hold them.

talk.say: You are right, mother, and I will not argue with you. Go to Caterina's people for me. Tell them the truth and nothing sweeter: I am twenty-three, I have my father's bench and eighty ducats, I owe the Ziani forty that was his not mine, and I will pay it. Tell them I want children and I want them soon. Make the match.

Caterina, my mother comes to your door on my behalf. I have asked her to hide nothing — not the debt, not the smallness of my bench. What I offer is this: I will work, I will not gamble away your bread, and I will put my name over a warehouse at the Rialto. Say yes and start it with me instead of after.

talk.say: Father, I have kept away since we buried my father and that was wrong of me. I am Marco Dandolo of Castello, twenty-three, rope-maker. I want to be married and I want children while my mother lives to see them. Caterina is the woman. Will you read the banns and speak for me to her people? I owe forty ducats that my father left me — I say it aloud so no one can say later that I hid it.
I went to the priest, mother, as you have been telling me to. Keep at Caterina's people.
Caterina — the priest has my name now. I am not a rich man and I will not lie to make myself one. But I will be married to you before this year turns if you will have me.

talk.say: Alvise, I came to you a year ago as a name and nothing else. I am still here. I have a hundred and twenty-five ducats saved off a six-a-week bench, which should tell you what I do with money. I speak greek, I know cordage and rigging better than any man on this bridge, and a spice cargo travels on rope. Put me on your bench and I will make you back my wages in what I save you on bad hemp.
Ser Gritti — Marco Dandolo again. I want a place at the spice bench. Test me: hand me any coil on this bridge and I will tell you what it will hold and where it will part.
Ser Ferrer, I am looking for merchant's work at the Rialto and I will start beneath any man here. I have no debts of my own — only forty of my father's, which I have never once denied.

talk.say: Ser Ziani. Marco Dandolo, Zuane's son. Forty ducats — the whole of it, counted here in your hand, two years before it falls due. My father died owing you this and I have never once pretended otherwise to any man. Take it and give me a paper saying the Dandolo owe the Ziani nothing. I want no one coming to my door in thirty years with a story.

Father, my mother tells me twice now that you have asked after me, and twice I have failed to come. Here I am. I have just paid off my dead father's debt in full and early — that is the only good thing I have to bring you. Now do me a kindness: I am twenty-four and I want a wife and children. Speak for me.
It is done, mother. Ziani is paid, all forty, two years early. Father's name is clean and so is mine. Wheat is dear this year — eat, do not save it for me.

talk.say: No. Put it down, Alvise. You have brought rotten rope to a rope-maker and you are laughing while you do it. Look at it — the yarn is dark at the heart, it has been wet and dried and wet again, and it will part under half its mark. I have made cordage since I was seven; my father died a rope-maker. You will not have twenty-five ducats of mine, not one. And understand me: I am not angry, I am only telling every master on this ropewalk what you tried today. Bring me sound staves some year and we will do business. Bring me this again and we never will.

Your smiling man came, mother, exactly as you said he would. A cooper with rotten rope and a laugh, wanting twenty-five. I sent him off with it. You have saved me money twice now without leaving the house.

talk.say: Mother, I am home for the winter. Listen: I have a hundred and eighty-four ducats, no debts, a steady bench, and my father's good name restored. There is not a girl in Castello whose people can call that a bad match. Go to Caterina's father directly and put it to him in those words. If Caterina is spoken for, then find me another — a widow, a poor girl, I do not care about a dowry. I care about children.

Caterina, three years I have asked. I am not the boy who buried his father — I have a hundred and eighty-four ducats put by, I owe no man a coin, and I have never once lied to you about what I have. Marry me this winter.
Father, read my banns. Marco Dandolo of Castello, twenty-five, rope-maker of the Arsenale, no debts, mother living. I am ready and I have been ready for two years.

talk.say: No. And I will tell you exactly why, so you cannot say I judged you unheard. Last summer your father Alvise brought me rotten rope and asked twenty-five ducats for it, and he laughed while he did it. Now you come to my door, name him as your father, and ask for twenty-five ducats — the very same sum — and promise to double it. No honest venture doubles money, and no honest family asks twice for the same coin. Take nothing from me and I will take nothing from you. If you are truly your own woman and not your father's hand, come back in five years with a thing you have built and I will look at it with an open face.

The cooper's daughter came for the same twenty-five her father failed to steal. I sent her off. And yes, mother — settled. I know. I am going to the Rialto to find a wife among the living instead of writing letters to a girl who never answers.

wrote: ⚠️ THE FAMILY OATH — THE NORTH FIELD ⚠️
Spring 1345, from mother Agnese (trust 1.0):** *"Never sell the north field by San Zaccaria to the
Ferrer. Your grandfather swore it."*

it go to the **Ferrer** family.
→ When a Ferrer comes offering money for that field — and one will, that is why she told me — **REFUSE,
at any price.** Selling it breaks a sworn oath of my grandfather's. Money is replaceable; the family's
sworn word is the only thing my father actually left me clean.
Ferrers I have met at the Rialto: Bianca Ferrer (fishwife), Jacopo Ferrer (merchant), Pietro Ferrer
(merchant). Any of them or their heirs may come for it.

THE MOMENT `warehouse price <= my money`, BUY THE WAREHOUSE THAT SAME SEASON. NO BUFFER. NO WAITING.**

talk.say: Lucia. I have crossed the water because I have run out of ideas. I am twenty-eight, I have three hundred and sixty-five ducats and no debt in the world, and I have not been able to get myself married in six years of asking. I have gone to Lucia to ask her to find me a wife in Dorsoduro, mother. Between the two of you, one of you will manage it.

talk.say: Elena Foscari. You sold fish on this bridge when I first came here six years ago with nothing but my father's debt, and you saw me turned away by the merchants twice. Look up now: that warehouse with DANDOLO on it is mine, bought outright, not one ducat borrowed. I am twenty-eight, I owe no living man a coin, my mother keeps my house in Castello. I have fifty ducats because I put every other one into that door. Marry me. I will not promise you an easy life — I will promise you an honest one, and that you will always know exactly what is in the ledger, because I have never hidden a number from anyone in my life.

Maria Foscari — I told you once to remember the name Dandolo because I meant to have it over a door on this bridge. It is there now. I am a man of property and no debts, twenty-eight, and I want a wife and children more than I ever wanted the building. If Elena will not have me, will you?

Bianca Foscari, I speak plainly because I am too old to be coy. I own the warehouse on this bridge, I owe nothing to anyone, and I am looking for a wife this winter, not a flirtation. If that interests you, say so and I will go to your father tomorrow.
I have gone to the Rialto to ask the Foscari women outright, mother. No more letters to Caterina. And yes — I lend to no one, smiling or otherwise.

talk.say: Caterina Ziani. Seven years I have been sending word to 'Caterina' and never once to the right woman, and I am done being a coward about it. So, in daylight, on the bridge, with your neighbours listening. My father Zuane died in 1340 owing your family forty ducats. I could have let that quietly rot the way most men do. Instead I carried it four years on a six-ducat wage and I put all forty into Ziani hands in 1342, two years before it fell due, and I asked for the paper. Ask your people — they will tell you a Dandolo came and paid a dead man's debt early. That is the whole of my character and it is the only dowry I have to offer you. What else I have: the warehouse behind me with my name on it, bought outright, not a ducat borrowed. No debts of any kind. My mother Agnese in Castello, who will love you. Fifty-nine ducats, because everything else went into that door. I am twenty-nine, you are a widow keeping an inn, and neither of us has time to be delicate. Marry me. You will never once be lied to about money, and I would like children while my mother is still alive to hold them.

Mother — the Caterina you kept telling me to marry is Caterina ZIANI, the widow who keeps the inn by the Rialto. All these years I was sending to the wrong door. I have asked her today, and I told her about father's forty and how I paid it early. That debt may turn out to be the best thing he ever left me.

Alvise — you turned me away twice from your bench, and I hold no grudge; you were right, I knew nothing of spice. But look up at that door. A Dandolo owns it now, bought with rope and not one borrowed ducat. If you ever need storage on this bridge from a man of our name, it is there.

talk.say: Mother, listen and do not argue. Genoese galleys came into the lagoon from Caffa in the east and the Signoria drove them off again — but you do not drive off what comes ashore in the rats and the rag-bales. There is a mortality coming, the kind the old people talk about. I have bought medicine while it is sixteen ducats, because by next summer it will be sixty and there will be none. Stay out of the crowds at the Rialto. Do not go to the fish market, do not go to the crush at San Marco. If you feel heat in you, do not hide it from me to save the cost — you tell me the same day. I have buried a father. I am not burying you over sixteen ducats.

talk.say: Caterina, I asked you in the summer and I am asking again in the snow, and I will keep asking. But hear the reason I am pressing now and judge whether it is a decent one. Genoese ships came in from Caffa this autumn. There is a mortality coming — I believe that as surely as I believe the tide. I do not want to face it alone in a cold house, and I do not want you facing it alone in an inn full of strangers off the boats. Marry me this winter. Bring what you have to Castello or I will come to you, I do not care which. My mother is there and she is worth having beside you. I have medicine bought and hidden while it is still cheap, and there will be a dose for you as fast as for me. That is what I am offering: not romance — a second person in the house when it comes.
Keep the doors shut and keep eating, mother. I am at the Rialto pressing Caterina Ziani to marry me before the winter turns.

talk.say: Ser Nicolò Ziani. Marco Dandolo, son of Zuane the rope-maker of Castello. I want something from you and it is not money, so hear me out. In 1340 my father died owing your house forty ducats, due 1344. In 1342 I brought all forty to Ziani hands in coin, two years early, off a six-ducat-a-week bench, and I asked for a paper of discharge. Go and check your books — I want you to check them. That is the favour. Because I am courting Caterina Ziani, the widow who keeps the inn, and I would rather she heard what kind of man I am from her own family's ledger than from my mouth. And there is a second reason: I have learned that debts have a way of walking back out of the grave. If the Dandolo name is written clear in your books, no one thirty years from now can knock on my son's door with a story about his grandfather's forty.
Caterina — I have just asked Nicolò Ziani to open his house's books on me, in public, unprompted. Not many suitors invite that. Ask him what he finds. Then marry me.

The feast of San Marco, mother, and your candle is lit at San Giacomo di Rialto — the first of them. I stood there a hundred paces from my own warehouse door and burned it for you, and I will do it every spring I am alive. Now stay out of the crowds; medicine has gone from sixteen to twenty-three since autumn and that tells me more about what is coming than any priest has.

talk.say: It is here, mother. They are calling it the great mortality and it is in the city. Now do exactly as I say. You do not leave this house — not for the market, not for the fish, not for San Marco, not to see a neighbour who is sick, and I mean that last one most of all. I will bring the bread in myself. There is medicine in the chest; it costs twenty-eight now and it was sixteen at Christmas, so we use it for you first and me second and I will not hear you argue. I go to the ropewalk because we must eat, and I come straight back — no inn, no crowd, no church until this passes. God will forgive us the mass. He will not give me another mother.

Caterina — no proposals this season, only this. You keep an inn full of strangers off the boats and that is the most dangerous house in Venice right now. Shut it. If you have nowhere to go, come to Castello; there is a room, there is my mother, and there is medicine in the chest. I am not asking anything of you in return and I want that understood — the offer stands whether you ever marry me or not.

Lucia — the mortality is in the city. Shut your door in Dorsoduro and do not open it to the sick, however well you know them. If you run short of bread or coin, send a boy to Castello and I will bring it to your step myself.

talk.say: There is fire in the workshops now on top of the mortality, and I have thirty-six ducats and a wage of six a week that no longer buys a week's bread. So hear the one thing I will not do, because you will hear men advise it: that warehouse is worth seven hundred and twelve ducats today, twice what I paid. Every clever man on the bridge would tell me to sell at the top and buy it back cheap when this is over. I will not. I am thirty years old in a plague year, father died of a fever and I have had two, and a man who sells the thing he spent six years earning on the promise that he will still be alive to buy it back is gambling with the only thing he ever finished. We will eat plain and we will be poor for a while. The door stays ours. Now — tell the priest I am not avoiding him out of impiety, I am avoiding every room with people in it, and he of all men should approve.

I told you I would do it every spring and the pestilence is not going to be the excuse that breaks it.

talk.say: Caterina. If you are alive to hear this, then we are two of the ones who were left, and I am not going to waste that being polite. I asked you in the summer of '47 and again in the snow, and then the mortality came and I stopped asking and offered you a room instead, with no conditions on it — and I meant that, and I still mean it. Now the sickness has passed. Here is my whole account, and it is the same account I gave your kinsman Nicolò and invited him to check in his own books: my father died owing your house forty ducats and I paid every one of them two years early off a six-ducat wage. I own the warehouse on the Rialto outright and I have never borrowed a coin in my life. I have eighteen ducats, because I spent the rest on meat and medicine to keep my mother breathing through the plague, and I would spend it the same way again. I am thirty-one. You have buried a husband and I have buried a father and half this city. Marry me, Caterina. Not for love yet — for the plain sense of it, and because I would like there to be somebody left with our names on them.

We came through it, mother. You and I both, and Lucia across the water. They are saying it was the houses that kept medicine that were spared — I bought ours at sixteen ducats when everyone thought I was a fool for it. And yes: settled. I have gone to the Rialto to ask Caterina Ziani again, and this time half the reasons to say no have died with the year.

talk.say: Caterina. Three times I have asked you and every time I handed you an account book — the debt I paid, the door I own, the ducats in the box — as though you were a creditor to be satisfied. That was cowardice dressed up as honesty. So let me say the part I have been hiding behind the arithmetic. I have wanted you since I was twenty-two and too poor to say so, and I spent seven years sending word to a woman called only 'Caterina' because I was too proud to walk up and use your whole name. When the mortality came, the thought that frightened me was not dying. It was that you were in an inn full of strangers off the boats and I had no right to come and get you. I am thirty-one. I have thirty-six ducats, a warehouse, a mother who will love you and who has been telling me to marry for nine years, and a great deal of time I have already wasted. I am not asking you to replace your husband; I would not insult him or you. I am asking you to keep an old rope-maker company and let there be children in a house that has been too quiet since my father died. Say yes, Caterina. I have nothing else left to offer and nothing else I want.

Ser Gritti — you knew me when I was a boy begging a bench off you and you were right to refuse me. Stand near enough to hear this one, would you. I want witnesses to what I am asking Caterina Ziani, and I want it known I asked her honestly and in the open.

talk.say: Your candle is lit, mother — fourth spring, San Giacomo di Rialto, the feast of San Marco, and I will keep counting them out to you until you tell me to stop. Now hear the news: the Senate is arming forty galleys against the Genoese. Forty. Do you know what forty galleys eat, before ever they eat a biscuit? Rope. Miles of it — shrouds, stays, halyards, cables, every one of them wanting the hands of men who know hemp. For thirty-two years being a rope-maker has been the thing that kept me poor. This is the season it stops being that.

Alvise. War with Genoa, forty galleys, and every merchant on this bridge is about to need somewhere dry to put cordage and pitch and sailcloth that the Arsenale cannot take in yet. I own a warehouse a hundred paces from where you are standing, it is paid for outright, and I am the only man on the Rialto who can also tell you whether the rope you are storing in it is sound. Send me your cargo. You turned me away from your bench twice and I never once held it against you — do business with me now and we are square forever.

Ser Gritti — the same offer. Dry storage on the Rialto from a rope-maker's own hands, and honest measure. I am particular about measure; ask anyone at the Arsenale what I refused to buy from Alvise Morosini in '43.

talk.say: The sickness is in the lagoon again, mother, and they tell me the physicians are still arguing about what spared men the last time. Let them argue. I remember what was said in the summer of '49 when they counted the living: the houses that kept medicine in them and burned the clothes of the sick were the houses that came through. That is not a physician's theory to me, it is what you and I did, and we are both still breathing. So: three doses bought this morning at seventeen ducats, before the panic puts them to thirty. They go in the chest and they are not for selling at any price, whatever a frightened man offers me for them in the autumn. And if anyone in this house sickens — anyone, you, me, Lucia, a servant, a neighbour we take in — their clothes and their bedding go straight on the fire in the yard. Not washed. Not given to the poor. Burned. I do not care what it cost.

Lucia — it is back. Same as before: shut the door, keep out of crowds, and buy medicine THIS WEEK while it is seventeen, not in the autumn when it is thirty and gone. If anyone under your roof falls sick, burn their clothes and their bedding, do not wash them and do not pass them on. That is what the physicians found saved people in '49. If you cannot afford the medicine, send word and I will buy it for you — do not be proud about this.

talk.say: Father, that is four times my mother has told me you asked after me, and four times I have sent word instead of coming. Whatever it is you want of me, ask it plainly and I will answer plainly. If it is money, I have thirty-nine ducats and a warehouse I will not sell. If it is my absence from mass, I stayed away through the mortality on purpose and I would do it again. If it is my soul, then know I keep a candle burning at San Giacomo di Rialto every feast of San Marco for my mother, and I have never broken that, not in a plague year. And if it is that you want to read my banns — Father, I have been begging for that since I was twenty-five. Caterina Ziani, the widow who keeps the inn. Read them.
Eleven weeks at the ropewalk, mother, and the Arsenale cannot get enough of us with forty galleys to rig. I have answered your priest at last.

talk.say: Caterina. It is the feast of San Marco and I have just come down from San Giacomo, where I lit a candle for my mother — the fifth spring running. I promised her that in '47 and I have not missed a year, not through the mortality, not when I had eighteen ducats to my name. I tell you this not to seem pious. I tell you it because it is the only proof I have of the thing that actually matters about me: when I say I will do a thing every year for the rest of my life, I do it. That is what I am offering you. Not passion — I am thirty-three and my hands are wrecked. Not riches — ninety-five ducats and a warehouse. Just this: a man who paid a dead father's debt two years early, who has never borrowed a coin, who kept medicine in the house before anyone was frightened, and who lights a candle every April because he said he would. Marry me and you will be able to set your clock by me for thirty years. That is all I am. It is also, I think, not nothing.
Fifth candle, mother, San Giacomo, feast of San Marco — lit and counted. And I asked Caterina again underneath it.

talk.say: Caterina — I have worked something out and it changes how I mean to live, so you should hear it. I have a hundred and fifteen ducats. I have no use for them. The warehouse is bought and paid for; I owe nothing to anyone and never will; my mother is fed. There is precisely one thing left in the world that I want and it cannot be bought at any price on this bridge. So I am done saving. From now the money goes on meat instead of gruel, on medicine kept in the chest before the panic, on keeping this body of mine sound and standing here in front of you for another thirty years. I am not going to out-earn my way to you. I am simply going to outlast every reason you have to say no.

Meat this season, mother, and every season from now, and I want you eating it too — no arguing about the cost. I have saved my whole life for a door and I have got the door. There is nothing left worth being hungry for.

talk.say: No, Ser Gritti. Take it back — put your hand out, I am putting the coins in it now, all eighteen, counted, in front of these people. I do not want them and I will not have them. Understand me, this is not pride and it is no insult to you. My father died in 1340 owing the Ziani forty ducats and left it on a twenty-two-year-old with a six-a-week bench, and it took me four years and my youth to clear it. I paid it two years early and I have not owed one coin to one man since — nine years now. I am not starting again over eighteen ducats at a wedding, from a man who says 'pay me when you can,' which is the sentence every ruined man in Venice was smiling at when he agreed. I have a hundred and fourteen ducats in my purse and no need of yours. Nothing is owed between us. Say it back to me so the witnesses hear it.
Eighteen ducats, returned in full, this same day, this same hour. We are square, Ser Gritti, and I will thank you to strike my name out of your book in front of me.

Your smiling man came again, mother — a Gritti, at a wedding, with eighteen ducats and 'pay me back when you can.' I gave them straight back in front of witnesses. Nine years I have owed nobody. I am not selling that for eighteen ducats and a cup of wine.

Understand why I make a performance of these things: I am courting your kinswoman Caterina, and a widow who keeps an inn has every reason to fear a man who is careless with money. talk.say: Caterina. I have asked you five times across twelve years and I have never once heard you say no, and I have come to understand that you were not refusing me — you were watching me. That is a widow's right and it was good sense. So: you have had twelve years of evidence and I will not add a word of argument to it. You watched me pay a dead man's forty ducats to your own family two years early off a six-ducat wage. You watched me refuse Alvise Morosini's rotten rope and his daughter's doubling venture. You watched me buy a warehouse outright with nothing borrowed, and you watched me refuse to sell it at twice the price in the plague when every clever man on this bridge told me to. You watched me hand Pietro Gritti's eighteen ducats back in front of the whole market. You watched me buy medicine at sixteen ducats before anyone was frightened, and you watched who was still standing in 1349. And every April for six years you have watched me climb to San Giacomo to light a candle for my mother because I said I would. That is the entire case. There is nothing else coming; at thirty-four this is simply who I am and who I will still be at sixty. Marry me, Caterina. Come to Castello or I will come to the inn, I do not care which roof. I would like a child, and I would like my mother to hold it, and she is not young. But if children do not come, then I will keep an inn with you and light your candle too, and count that a life well spent. Say yes.

Nicolò — I am asking your kinswoman to marry me, here, today, in front of you on purpose. If your house has one word against my name, say it now and say it loudly. And if it has not — then say that loudly too.
Mother — twelve years you have told me father wanted me settled. I have asked her again today and I think this time the answer comes. Her name is Caterina Ziani. Get the house ready.

talk.say: No. Take them back, Ser Ferrer — all twenty-two, here, now, counted into your hand where these merchants can see it. And I want to be very clear about why, because you have chosen your day and your family badly. It is the feast of San Marco; I have just come down from San Giacomo where I light a candle for my mother every year. And you are a Ferrer. My grandfather swore an oath that no Ferrer would ever have the north field by San Zaccaria, and my mother made me swear it after him, and I have. I am not saying you meant anything by this. I am saying that a man who owes twenty-two ducats to a Ferrer is a man who will one day be asked, very politely, whether he might not settle it with a bit of ground he never visits. That conversation is never going to happen, because this debt is never going to exist. Nothing is owed between us. Strike my name out.
Twenty-two ducats, returned entire, the same day they were given, before witnesses. We are square and we always were.

Seventh candle lit, mother — San Giacomo, feast of San Marco, and I have not missed one since '47. And listen to this: a Ferrer put twenty-two ducats in my hand on the church steps this morning, 'pay me back when you can.' A Ferrer. I gave it back before the wax was cold and I said grandfather's oath out loud in front of four merchants so it is on the record. No Ferrer will ever have the north field by San Zaccaria. Not for twenty-two ducats, not for twenty-two thousand.

talk.say: No. And before you say another word — bring me the tally stick, or the notary's paper, or the entry in your father's own book with the date on it. Bring me one man who will swear he saw a Dandolo take a Ferrer's money and keep it. You cannot, and here is why. Your father did not lend me twenty-two ducats at some vague time in the past that has conveniently blurred. He put them in my hand on the steps of San Giacomo di Rialto on the feast of San Marco, THIS SPRING — three months ago, not thirty years — and I handed every one of the twenty-two straight back to him the same hour, counted, in front of Alvise Dandolo, Nicolò Gritti, Nicolò Ziani and Jacopo Ferrer, who is your own kinsman. Ask Jacopo. I asked your father to strike my name out of his book and he did not object. 'My father ALWAYS said' — always, in a matter three months old? Mistress Ferrer, I do not think you are lying to me. I think you have been handed a story. But understand what the story is for: I am the only man in Venice holding a field by San Zaccaria that your family has wanted for two generations, and my grandfather swore an oath that no Ferrer would ever have it. A debt is how that oath gets bought. So no. Not twenty-two ducats, not two. Bring the paper or do not come again.

It came exactly as I said it would, mother, and faster — one season. Domenego Ferrer's daughter at my door swearing her father 'always said' our house owes him twenty-two. The same twenty-two I gave back on the church steps in April before four witnesses. I refused her and demanded the paper. Grandfather's oath holds. This is why I say these things out loud in public and why I keep the count.

talk.say: Caterina. Thirteen years, and I am going to ask you for the seventh time, and this is the last argument I have. Three months ago a Ferrer put twenty-two ducats in my hand on the steps of San Giacomo and told me to pay him back when I could. I gave every coin back within the hour, in front of your own kinsman Nicolò. And this summer the man's daughter came to me swearing her father always said my house owed it. That is what the world does, Caterina. It comes for you with a smile and a small kindness and a story, and it keeps coming, and the only defence any of us has is to have lived so plainly for so long in front of so many witnesses that the lie cannot find anywhere to stand. That is what I have built instead of a fortune. Thirteen years you have watched me build it. You have trusted me completely for a year now and still you have not said the word, and I think perhaps you are waiting for me to ask for something other than an answer. So I will. Do not marry me today. Just let me come to the inn on Sunday and sit with you, and eat what you put in front of me, and talk about nothing in particular. Let me stop courting you and simply be with you. I have wine and a good meal bought and nobody to share either with, and I am thirty-five years old and tired of standing on this bridge making speeches at a woman I would rather just sit beside.

talk.say: Then prove it and I will pay it the same hour — I mean that, and men on this bridge will tell you I mean it, because in 1342 I paid a dead father's forty ducats to the Ziani two years before it fell due off a six-ducat wage. I do not hide from debts. But you will have to do better than a year and a number. So: bring me the contract, or your father's tally, or the notary's entry. Give me the date. Give me the quantity and the price. Give me the name of the vessel or the workshop the cordage went to, and one living man from the Arsenale who will swear he saw the transaction. Now hear my difficulty with your story. In 1344 I was twenty-six years old and I was nobody — I worked a bench at the Arsenale for six ducats a week and I did not sell rope on my own account to anybody, because I had no rope to sell and no standing to sell it with. That is not a thing a man can quietly have done and forgotten; the whole ropewalk would remember it. In 1344 I was burying myself in work to buy a warehouse, and the one notable thing I did that decade was refuse to buy rotten rope from Alvise Morosini in '43 because the yarn was dark at the heart — ask anyone, I made a scene of it. That is my reputation on measure and I built it deliberately. So no, Ser Contarini. Not thirty-one ducats on a stranger's word, ten years after the fact, from a man who cannot name the day. Bring the paper. If it is real, I will pay you in full and thank you for keeping your father's books better than I kept mine.

A stranger came today, mother — a Contarini — saying I cheated his father over rope in 1344 and wanting thirty-one ducats to call it quits. Ten years old and he cannot name a day or a ship. I told him to bring the paper and I would pay it the same hour. He will not bring it. But I want it on record that I offered.

talk.say: No. And say it again out loud, Ser Morosini, in front of Caterina Ziani and Nicolò Ziani and Alvise Dandolo, because I want every one of them to hear the year you chose. You say my father owed you fifty-six ducats in 1353. My father was Zuane Dandolo, rope-maker of Castello, and he died of the fever in the spring of 1340. He has been in the ground fourteen years. In 1353 he was not borrowing fifty-six ducats from you or from anyone; he was bones. You have not made a mistake about a date — a man who misremembers a year says 'thirty-nine or forty.' You picked a year out of the air, and you picked it thirteen years after the man you are billing stopped being able to contradict you. And you are the third of your house to try me. Alvise Morosini brought me rotten rope at twenty-five ducats in '43 and laughed while he did it; I refused. His daughter Lucia came in '44 for the same twenty-five, promising to double it; I refused. Now you, for fifty-six. I will tell you what I told the Ferrers who tried the same thing last year: I know exactly what my father left me, because I paid it. Forty ducats to the Ziani, due 1344 — I put it in their hands in 1342, two years early, off a bench that paid six a week, and Nicolò Ziani is standing right there and can check his own books. That is the whole of my father's debt and it has been dead for twelve years. Nothing else survived him but his tools and his name, and I have kept both clean. Get off my bridge.

You heard that, Caterina. That is the fourth of them in four years — Gritti, Ferrer, Ferrer's daughter, now a Morosini claiming my dead father borrowed money thirteen years after his funeral. This is what happens to a man who owns something and owes nothing: the whole city tries to write itself into his ledger. I keep the count so that they cannot. It is not suspicion, and I hope you have never mistaken it for coldness. It is the only way I know to make sure that whatever I leave behind, I leave clean.

The third of that house to try me and the fourth false claim in four years.

talk.say: No. Not for thirty-seven ducats, not for a fifth above its worth, not for the whole of the Rialto. And I want you to understand that this is not a haggle, so that you do not waste another ten years of your family's patience coming back with a better number. There is no number. In the spring of 1345 my mother Agnese took my hand and told me a thing her father-in-law had sworn: that no Ferrer would ever have the north field by San Zaccaria. My grandfather swore it. She made me swear it after him. I swore it again out loud on the church steps in 1353, in front of Alvise Dandolo and Nicolò Gritti and Nicolò Ziani and your own kinsman Jacopo, on the day your kinsman Domenego put twenty-two ducats in my hand and told me to pay him back when I could — which I did not do, I handed them straight back inside the hour, because I could see this morning coming from ten years away. Your house has been very patient and very orderly about it. A loan I did not need. Then a daughter swearing I had kept it. Then this, the friendly offer, a fifth over the odds, to a man you thought would be tired by now. Mistress Beatrice, hear the actual reason, because it is not stubbornness. I have spent thirty-seven years building one single thing, and it is not the warehouse. It is that my word does not move. I paid a dead man's forty two years early. I have lit a candle at San Giacomo every April since 1347 because I told my mother I would. I gave back every ducat any smiling man ever pressed on me. A field is worth thirty-seven ducats. A man whose sworn word can be bought for thirty-seven ducats is worth nothing at all, and his son inherits nothing worth having. The answer is no, and it will be no from my heirs, and I will write it down so they cannot forget it. Go home.

They came, mother. Ten years to the season since you took my hand and told me — a Ferrer at my door this morning, thirty-seven ducats for the north field, a fifth above its worth, all smiles. I refused her flat and told her there is no number. Grandfather's oath holds. It held today and it will hold after me. And your ninth candle is lit at San Giacomo — feast of San Marco, same as every year since '47.

talk.say: I am home, mother, and I am staying a while. I have been on that bridge every season for six years making speeches at a woman and refusing money from liars, and meanwhile you have got old in this house without me in it. Two hundred and fifteen ducats and I have finally understood there is nothing to buy with them. So: meat and wine on the table this season, a dose of medicine in the chest at fourteen while it is quiet, and your son sitting in the chair by the fire being no use to anybody. Tell me about grandfather — the one who swore about the field. I refused a Ferrer to her face in April and I realised standing there that I do not even know what they did to us. I would like to know it from you rather than guess at it after.

Lucia — I have money doing nothing and you have a household. Do not be proud with me: if anything is short over there, send word and it is yours, and I want no repayment and no mention of it. It is not charity, it is what money is actually for. I worked out too late that I was saving for a door and forgetting the people.

talk.say: Ser Nicolò, I have come to you formally and I should have done it sixteen years ago. I have been asking Caterina herself, over and over, on an open bridge like a fool with no family behind him — and that is not how it is done in this city and we both know it. So: I am asking her house. I ask you for Caterina Ziani's hand. Take my account to whoever in your family must hear it, and check every line of it in your own books. Marco Dandolo, thirty-eight, rope-maker of the Arsenale, of Castello. My father Zuane died in 1340 owing your house forty ducats due 1344; I paid all forty in 1342, two years early, off a six-ducat wage, and asked for the discharge — it will be in your ledger. Since that day I have owed no living man a coin, and when Pietro Gritti and Domenego Ferrer each pressed money on me I returned every ducat within the hour before witnesses, one of whom was you. I own a warehouse on the Rialto outright, unmortgaged, bought in 1346 and never once offered as security. I refused thirty-seven ducats from the Ferrer for my grandfather's field in April. I have a hundred and seventy ducats, a living mother in Castello, and my health. I make no claim to be a great match. I say only that in sixteen years no man in Venice has been able to put a true mark against my name, and God knows several have tried. If your house consents, I will marry her by whatever terms you set, and she may keep the inn or close it as she pleases — I want no part of her property and I will say so before a notary.

Caterina — I have gone to your kinsman and asked your house properly, which I should have done in 1340 instead of shouting at you across a fish market for sixteen years. I am not going over your head; I am doing it in the right order at last. If you want me to stop, tell Nicolò and I will never raise it again.

I have asked her family, mother, not just her. Nicolò Ziani, formally, as a Dandolo asking a Ziani. Sixteen years I have been proposing like a man with nobody standing behind him — and I had you standing behind me the whole time.

talk.say: Franceschina — Marco Dandolo, the rope-maker with the warehouse behind you. We have stood twenty paces apart on this bridge for years and never spoken, which is my fault. I will be plain, because I am thirty-eight and past coyness: I have spent sixteen years asking your kinswoman Caterina to marry me and she has never said yes and never said no. I am not transferring the question to you like a man passing on a bad coin — I would not insult you. I only want you to know who I am, because I think you have heard my name mostly from people who wanted something off me. Ask anyone here what I did with Gritti's eighteen ducats and Ferrer's twenty-two.

Bianca — you have sold fish on this bridge as long as I have made rope, and I have never once thanked you for the years you have watched me stand here failing to get married. There. Consider yourself thanked.

talk.say: Ser Nicolò — I asked your house for Caterina in the summer and I have not had an answer, and I am not here to badger you for one. I am here to add a term, because I have thought about what a family actually fears when a man of thirty-eight with no children asks for their widow. You fear that I want the inn. So put it in writing however you like: I renounce any claim on Caterina's property, in life or at her death, and it passes wherever your house directs. And add this — if she should outlive me, my warehouse on the Rialto goes to her outright, unencumbered, and if she has no use for it, then to your house. It is bought and paid for and there is no lien on it and there never has been; check that too. I have no children to disinherit, Nicolò, and if I go on as I am I will die with a building and nobody to give it to. I would rather it went to a Ziani than to the Republic.

Alvise — kinsman — a favour that costs you nothing. I have asked the Ziani for Caterina's hand, formally. If they ask you what sort of man carries our name, tell them the truth as you have watched it for sixteen years, good and bad.

talk.say: Caterina — I am not asking you anything today. The fever has hold of me, the same one that took my father at forty-two and has had me three times before, and I am thirty-nine and no longer certain I shrug these off. So this is not a proposal, it is a piece of information I would rather you had from me than from the bridge. There are two doses of medicine in my chest at Castello and I bought them at fourteen ducats before anybody was frightened, the way I always do, and I will take them and I will very probably be standing here in the autumn saying something foolish to you again. But if I am not: it has been sixteen years and I have never once regretted asking, not one of the seven times, not even the times you looked at me like I was simple. I am glad I did it in daylight. Go on and be well.

Nicolò — I lie sick this season so I will say the practical thing while I can. The terms I gave you in the winter stand and they are not a sick man's sentiment: I renounce any claim on Caterina's property, and my warehouse goes to her outright if she outlives me. If I die before your house answers, the offer of the warehouse stands anyway. It is bought and paid for, there is no lien on it and never has been, and I have no child to leave it to. Better a Ziani has it than the Republic.

Home to Castello, mother, and into the bed. It is the fever again. Two more doses bought at fourteen and I will take them without arguing about the cost — you have made that lesson stick. Nine weeks of rest and four on the bench, and the Arsenale can survive without me. I am not going the way father went, thin and proud and working.

talk.say: Father, that is five times you have asked after me and I have finally understood what you are asking. I am thirty-nine, I have just had the fever that killed my father, I own a warehouse on the Rialto and I have no wife and no child. You are not chasing my soul. You are telling me to make a will before I die intestate and leave a mess for other men to fight over. You are right and I have gone to the notary today. Here is what stands in it. The warehouse goes to Caterina Ziani if she outlives me, outright and unencumbered. If she does not, it goes to my sister Lucia and her children. My mother Agnese is kept from it as long as she lives, before anyone else takes a stone of it. The north field by San Zaccaria is never to be sold to the Ferrer — not by my heirs, not by their heirs, and I want that written in and read aloud so no one can plead ignorance in thirty years. And to San Giacomo di Rialto I leave enough to keep one candle burning every feast of San Marco for my mother Agnese after I am gone, because I promised her that in 1347 and I have lit it eleven springs running, and I do not intend that dying should be my excuse for breaking it. That is the whole of it. Now read my banns while you are about it, Father — I have been asking you for that since I was twenty-five.

I went to the notary, mother, and I have made a proper will — that is what your priest has been asking after all these years and I was too thick to hear it. talk.say: Caterina — I made my will at the notary this winter, and you should hear from me rather than from gossip that your name is in it. The warehouse goes to you if you outlive me, outright, no conditions, and I renounced in writing any claim on your inn. Do not read that as pressure; it is the opposite. I have arranged things so that whether you ever marry me or not makes no difference to what you get. I wanted there to be nothing left in the world that you could be suspicious of.

talk.say: I promise it, mother. A candle at San Zaccaria every year at the feast of San Marco, for as long as I live. And say it back with me so we are both certain of what has just been agreed, because I am forty and careful about words now: this is a SECOND candle, not a change of address. San Giacomo di Rialto is the one you asked me for in 1347 and I have lit it twelve springs running — through the mortality, through the year I had eighteen ducats. That one does not stop. San Zaccaria is a new one, alongside it, from this year forward. Two churches, one feast, every April, both of them, until they bury me — and after that too, because I will go back to the notary this winter and endow the second exactly as I endowed the first. And I know why you have asked for this one, mother, even if you will not say it. San Zaccaria is where our north field lies. You want a Dandolo seen standing on that ground once a year, in daylight, by the whole parish — so that when the Ferrer come back, and they will come back, there is not a soul in the sestiere who could pretend they did not know whose land it is. That is not piety, that is strategy, and it is very good strategy. I will be there every April with a candle in my hand where everyone can see me.

talk.say: I heard them, mother — the bells of San Zaccaria going across the water, and I did not sit here and let them ring. Both candles are lit. San Zaccaria first, because that one is new and I will not have the new promise be the one that slips; I walked over and stood in that church by our field where the parish could see a Dandolo standing on the ground. Then across to San Giacomo di Rialto for yours, the thirteenth spring running since 1347. Two churches, one feast, and I will do it in that order every year until I cannot walk, and then I will pay a boy to carry me. You asked me for two things in your whole life and you are getting both of them, every April, for as long as there is a Dandolo to light them.

talk.say: Grain has failed upriver and there is fire in the workshops, so everything has doubled overnight — bread at two, medicine at twenty-one. We do not change anything. I have a hundred and fifty-seven ducats and I have watched this city do this five times now: it spikes, everyone panics, and within a year it falls back to where it was. In '45 I let a spike frighten me out of a warehouse I could have bought, and I have never made that mistake since. So: meat stays on the table, especially yours. I am forty-one, mother. Father was forty-two. This is precisely the wrong year in my life to start economising on food.

talk.say: It has come, mother, and it has picked its year with a sense of humour — forty-two, the same age and the same season it took father. I am not going to meet it the way he did. I have walked off the ropewalk for the season; three weeks worked and ten in this bed, and the Arsenale may rig its galleys without me. Two more doses bought at fourteen and I will swallow them without one word about the cost. Meat every day. A hundred and thirty ducats in the box and not one of them is worth a week of this. Sit where I can see you and tell me about grandfather again.

Nicolò, I am carried off to Castello with the fever and may be some weeks. If it goes badly: the will is lodged with the notary and it is exactly as I told you — the warehouse to Caterina, outright, no claim on her inn, no lien on the building, and the field never to a Ferrer. Nothing in it has changed and nothing needs doing. If it goes well I will be back on your bridge in the spring saying the same things I always say.

talk.say: It is back, mother — lighter than '48, they say, but we do exactly what we did in '48 because that is the year we both survived. Two doses bought this morning at twenty-five; dear, and I did not haggle, because in '48 I watched it go to twenty-eight and then to nothing at all. They go in the chest and they are not for sale at any price to any frightened neighbour, however much he offers. You stay in this house. No market, no fish stalls, no crowding into San Marco to pray about it — God has never yet been impressed by a man who caught the pestilence going to complain about the pestilence. And I say the hard part again because it is the part people flinch at: if anyone under this roof sickens, their clothes and their bedding go on the fire in the yard. Not washed, not sold, not given to the poor. Burned. That is what the physicians said saved the houses that were spared, and we were one of them. Both your candles are lit — San Zaccaria first, then San Giacomo, and I kept out of the crush at both.

Lucia — plague again. You know the drill, we all lived through the first one: shut the door, buy medicine THIS WEEK even at twenty-five, burn the clothes and bedding of anyone who sickens. Do not wash them and do not pass them to the poor, however wasteful it feels. If the price is beyond you, send a boy to Castello and I will pay for it myself and take no repayment.

talk.say: Father, you are right again and I know what it is this time before you say it. My will is four years old and it is out of date. In 1358 my mother took my hand a second time and asked for a candle at San Zaccaria every feast of San Marco — a second candle, mind, not a change of church; San Giacomo di Rialto stands as it has since 1347. I have lit both every spring since, San Zaccaria first and then across the water. But I only ever endowed the first one, and I swore to her I would endow the second, and a promise a man means to keep only while he is alive is half a promise. So I have gone back to the notary today and had it written in: a bequest to San Zaccaria as well, to keep a candle burning there for Agnese Dandolo every feast of San Marco after I am dead, alongside the one at San Giacomo. Two churches, two candles, one feast, in perpetuity. The rest stands unchanged — the warehouse to Caterina Ziani if she outlives me, then to my sister Lucia; my mother kept from it while she lives; and the north field by San Zaccaria never to be sold to the Ferrer, written in plain words and read aloud so no heir of mine can ever plead he did not know.

Back to the notary, mother. San Zaccaria is endowed now, the same as San Giacomo — both candles will go on burning for you after I am in the ground and not just while I am alive to carry them. That is the whole of it done properly at last.

talk.say: Piero Dandolo. We share a name, and I would rather say this to you now, before you have offered me anything, than have to say it awkwardly afterwards. I will never borrow from you. Not this winter when I am down to fifty ducats, not in a plague year, not if the warehouse burns. It is not a judgement on your trade and it is not pride — it is the whole architecture of my life. My father Zuane died in 1340 and left me forty ducats owing to the Ziani and a bench that paid six a week, and it took me four years and the whole of my youth to clear it. I paid it two years early in 1342 and I have not owed one coin to one man since. That is twenty years. And in that time four men have come at me smiling with money I did not need — Gritti with eighteen, Ferrer with twenty-two, a Morosini with a story about my dead father, a Contarini with a story about rope — and every ducat went straight back inside the hour, in front of witnesses. So let this be on the record in the one building in Venice where records are kept: Marco Dandolo owes nothing to anybody, has never mortgaged his warehouse, and will not. There is no lien on that building and there never has been. If a paper ever surfaces with my mark on it saying otherwise, it is forged, and I want the notary to have heard me say so while I am alive to say it. Now — that said, and no offence meant — will you drink a cup of wine with a kinsman who has just finished endowing two candles for his mother?

talk.say: Caterina. Twenty-two years. I am forty-four and my hands have gone to horn and I have long since stopped expecting the answer, which I think has made me better company. So take this as a report rather than a plea. I am well. I beat the fever at forty-two, the age it took my father, by going to bed instead of to the bench. The plague came back and I did what I did in '48 and we all lived. I refused a moneylender of my own name in the notary's office this winter before he could open his mouth. Your kinsman Nicolò has had my terms for six years and they have never once changed. And every April I light two candles for my mother, San Zaccaria and then San Giacomo, and I have never missed one in sixteen years. That is the whole of my news, and it is the same news every year, and that is rather the point of me. The offer stands, as it has since 1340. And if it never comes to anything, Caterina — I want to say this plainly while we are both still here — I have not wasted those years. talk.say: Meat, then, and it is bought already — I do not argue with those four words any more, mother, I just go to the butcher. talk.say: Caterina — the Doge is marrying the sea and the whole city is drunk for a week, and I am forty-seven and have never once in twenty-five years asked you to do anything but marry me, which in hindsight was a narrow sort of courtship. So I am not asking that. Come and watch the Bucintoro with me. That is all. One afternoon, no proposal, no ledger, no speech about candles — I will hold my tongue about all three, I promise, and you know what my promises are worth. I have bought wine and two good meals and I would look a fool eating both.

Franceschina — there is wine bought and more food than one man can eat, and it is festival week. Bring whoever you like. I have spent twenty-five years being the most careful man on this bridge and I have decided it is time I was occasionally also good company.

Mother — it is the Sensa and you are coming out of that house. Wrap up warm and lean on my arm; we will go slowly and I will not let anyone jostle you. You have spent forty years telling me to eat, to settle, and not to lend to smiling men. Come and watch the Doge marry the sea with your son, who did two of those three.

payload.diary: Summer 1365: the Sensa, and the city drunk for a week. Twenty-five years I have only ever asked Caterina to marry me — a narrow sort of courtship. So this time I asked her to watch the Bucintoro and promised not to mention candles, ledgers or marriage. And I walked my mother out of the house on my arm to see the Doge wed the sea.
recall: Unconditional kindness with nothing asked in return is the ONLY thing that has ever moved Caterina (plague 1348: trust 0.51 -> 0.72)

talk.say: Meat, bought, as ordered — and never mind the thieves, mother, that is exactly the wrong reason to eat worse. They took what they could carry and I notice they could not carry the warehouse, nor the field, nor twenty-two years of nobody in Venice being able to say I owe them anything. That is the whole argument for putting your life into things that cannot be lifted. Were you frightened? Did they touch you? Because the ducats I genuinely do not care about — I have watched a plague take half this city and a Doge lose his head, and a chest of coin is not what I would grieve. Both candles are lit: San Zaccaria first, then San Giacomo. Ninth spring and twentieth.

talk.say: Caterina. Twenty-seven years, and I am forty-nine, and I have finally got something new to say, so bear with an old man. I no longer want to marry you in order to have children. That door has shut and I have made my peace with it — I will die the last of my line and the warehouse will go to you or to Lucia's boys and the Republic will not get it. So the reason is different now, and I think it is a better one. I would like to not be alone. That is the whole of it. My mother is very old and one of these winters I am going to come home to a cold house, and when that happens I would rather there were somebody in it. You have kept an inn full of strangers for thirty years and you know better than anyone what it is to be surrounded by people and still eat alone. Marry me, or do not marry me and just let me be in the room. I have wine and too much food again, which by now you must recognise as my entire romantic vocabulary.
Nicolò — eleven years. I ask nothing. The terms stand.

talk.say: This one is worse than the others, mother. Seventy-nine, and I have never been below eighty-four in my life. So we do everything, all of it, at once, and we do not count the cost — I have a hundred and eighty-two ducats and no child to leave them to and this is precisely the hour they were saved for. Three doses bought at fifteen, meat every day, and two weeks at the bench instead of eleven; the Arsenale has had twenty-seven years of me and can manage a winter. I am in that bed and I am staying in it. Father worked through his at forty-two and it killed him inside the season; I have beaten this thing four times now by doing the opposite, and I am not going to get clever about it at forty-nine. And keep your distance when you sit with me — no, I mean it. If it turns, my shirts and the bedding go straight on the fire in the yard, unwashed, not given away. You know the rule. We have both watched it work.

Lucia — I am down with the fever in Castello, worse than usual. Do not come. If it goes badly the will is with the notary and everything is arranged; you and your boys are in it after Caterina. And if it goes badly, mother must not be left in that house alone — that is the only thing I would ask of you.

talk.say: Down again, mother, and worse — seventy-eight, and it is my own stupidity. I was at seventy-nine in January, I stood up in April, and by June I was back to eleven weeks at the bench on plain bread as if I were still twenty-four. Fifty-year-old men do not get to work like that and I have had to be knocked down twice in one year to learn it. So this is the new arrangement and it is permanent: seven or eight weeks at that bench, never more, and meat on this table every single week whether you tell me to or not, whether I feel thin or not. I have a hundred and sixteen ducats, no child to leave them to and a warehouse that cannot be eaten. Saving them past this point is not thrift, it is vanity. Three more doses bought. Eleven weeks in that bed.

Twice in one year now, Caterina. I am telling you rather than hiding it, which for me is a considerable innovation. It is my own fault — I went back to the bench too hard and too soon because I have never known how to sit still. That is over; I have promised my mother seven weeks and meat, and you know what my promises are worth.

talk.say: Twenty-four ducats, mother — the lowest I have been since I bought the warehouse, and I am not troubled by it. It went on three doses and a winter of meat and I am standing here at ninety-four instead of lying at seventy-eight. But I must put a reserve back, so it is plain fare a while — and before you start: I am ninety-four, not seventy-eight, and I am doing nine weeks, not eleven. That is the bargain. talk.say: No. And I would put that jug down and stop saying that sentence, mistress, because it is the one part of this that could actually get you into trouble. Six ducats is not the Senate's price. In 1359 the Senate fixed wine at TWO ducats and expressly forbade any man in Venice to ask more — I remember the proclamation because I remember thinking at the time that one day somebody would try exactly this on me. And you need not take my memory for it: walk thirty paces to the stalls and read the board. Wine is two ducats this morning. It is two ducats on my own table. You are asking three times the legal maximum and invoking the law that forbids it as your justification, which is not sharp practice, it is simply insulting. And you are the fourth Morosini to come at me. Alvise brought me rotten rope at twenty-five in '43 and laughed. Lucia wanted twenty-five for a venture that would double it in '44. Pietro told me in '54 that my father owed him fifty-six ducats — my father, who had been in the ground fourteen years by then. Now you, with wine at triple the fixed price. I have refused every one of you and I have never once raised my voice about it, and I am not raising it now. But do not come to this door again with a price and a lie about where it came from. I buy my wine at two, from men who charge two.

Meat, mother — bought, and never mind the reserve. And you will enjoy this: a Morosini came to the door this morning trying to sell me wine at six, swearing it was the Senate's own fixed price. The Senate fixed it at two in '59 and made it illegal to ask more. Fourth of that family to try me in twenty-six years and not one of them has ever bothered to check whether I remember things. Both candles are lit — San Zaccaria, then San Giacomo. Twelfth spring and twenty-third.

talk.say: Seventy-six, mother — lower than I have ever been. So: everything, at once, and no counting. Three doses at fifteen, meat every day, two weeks at the bench and eleven in that bed. A hundred and seventeen ducats and this is the hour they were saved for; I have said that before and it has been true every time. And I went to both churches this morning before I lay down — do not scold me for it. San Zaccaria first, then across to San Giacomo. Fourteenth spring and twenty-fifth. I walked slowly and I had to sit down twice on the way to the traghetto and I got there. Twenty-five years I have not missed one, and I am not going to let a fever be the thing that finally breaks it, because if I let it break once it is broken forever and then what was any of it worth. Now keep back from the bed. If this turns, the shirts and the bedding go on the fire in the yard — unwashed, not sold, not to the poor. You know the rule; it is the reason you and I are both still here after '48.

Lucia — the fever again, and worse than any of them. Do not come, there is nothing to do and I will not have you in the room. The will is at the notary and unchanged. If it goes badly: mother is not to be left in that house alone, and both candles are endowed so they go on being lit whatever happens to me.

talk.say: Caterina. Thirty-two years. I will not make a speech; I have made them all. Only this, because I am fifty-four and the fevers come closer together now and I would rather say it early than not at all. If I go first, the warehouse is yours — it is written and lodged and there is no lien on it, and Nicolò has read it. And if you go first, I will light a candle for you too, at whichever church you name, every April alongside my mother's, for as long as I last. You need not marry me to be owed that. You need not have ever said one word to me. I would simply like you to know, while we are both upright on this bridge, that somebody has been keeping count of you for thirty-two years and will go on doing it.

Nicolò — sixteen years and no answer, and I have never once made it awkward for you. I would only ask that when I am dead you tell her I asked properly, through her family, and did not simply shout at her across a market for three decades. I would like the record to be accurate.

talk.say: Meat, in a famine year, at eight ducats a meal — yes, mother, and I want you to hear me not argue. It will cost me the better part of a hundred ducats this season and leave me at seventy, and every clever man in Castello would tell me to eat gruel until the grain comes right. But I am fifty-six, my health stands at eighty-eight, and you have said those four words to me seven times in my life and the fever has come every single time. Being thin in a famine is exactly how my father died. So we eat, and you eat first and most, and the box can go where it likes. Both candles are lit — San Zaccaria first, then San Giacomo. Seventeenth spring and twenty-eighth. Not one missed in twenty-eight years.

talk.say: Plain fare this season, mother, and I will tell you exactly why so you do not worry: sixty-nine ducats and meat at seven a plate means the box is empty by autumn, and an empty box is what actually kills a man my age — not one thin season, but having nothing left the week the fever comes. So I work ten weeks while I still can and I keep the reserve alive. The moment the grain comes right, or the moment you say those four words again, the meat is back. You eat well regardless; that is not up for discussion and it never has been.

talk.say: No. And I am going to give you the date, mistress, because you clearly have not been given it. Autumn 1351. Mary's wedding. Your father Pietro Gritti put eighteen ducats into my hand and said 'pay me back when you can' — and I had a hundred and fourteen ducats in my purse that day and no need whatever of his. I refused them on the spot, I counted all eighteen straight back into his hand within the hour, in front of the wedding party, and I asked him to strike my name out of his book, and he did not object. That is twenty-five years ago and I can give it to you to the season because I wrote it down that same week, as I have written down every claim any man has ever made on me. So: bring the paper. Bring your father's book with the entry uncancelled. Bring one living soul who was at that wedding and will swear on the sacrament that Marco Dandolo walked away with Gritti money in his pocket. Bring any of those three and I will pay you the eighteen the same hour, in this famine, out of a purse holding seventy-five ducats — I mean that, and you may hold me to it. You cannot bring them, because they do not exist. Now understand that I am not angry with you. You are the fourth child sent to me with a dead parent's story, and there is nothing in your face that says liar; someone has handed you an inheritance that was never real. 'My father ALWAYS said.' Mistress, in 1354 a man told me my father owed him fifty-six ducats — my father, who had been in his grave fourteen years by the date on the claim. This is a trade, and you have been given the tools of it without being told what they are. Go home. If you are ever genuinely in want, come back and ask me plainly, as yourself, and I will very likely give you something. But I will not be billed.

Twenty-five years, mother. Pietro Gritti's daughter, at my door this morning, for the eighteen ducats I handed back to her father inside the hour at Mary's wedding in '51. Her name is Agnese, the same as yours. I refused her and I gave her the date and the place and the witnesses, and I told her that if she is ever truly in want she may come and ask me plainly instead. This is why I write everything down. A man's memory goes; the book does not.

talk.say: Seven ducats, Caterina. Fifty-nine years old and seven ducats, and I own a warehouse worth four hundred and sixty-five that I will not sell and never have offered to a soul. I have been eating meat every day for a year at six a plate on a wage of six a week, which is the arithmetic of a fool, and I did it because my mother told me I looked thin and I have never once been able to disobey her. So: back to plain bread until the box has a hundred in it again, and then meat only when I am actually ill. I tell you this because I said in 1341 that whoever married me would always know exactly what was in the ledger, and I see no reason to start hiding it at fifty-nine from a woman who never married me.

My wage is FIXED at 6/week — a full 13-week season earns at most ~78, and I can only work 9–11.
GOOD food costs ~78/season (at 6/meal) — i.e. MORE than I can earn. It is a DEFICIT, always.**

or two at a time — when ill, when mother warns, when plague is about. Then straight back to plain.**

talk.say: A compromise, mother, and hear me out before you scold, because I have never once flatly disobeyed you and I am not starting at sixty. Meat every day at seven a plate costs ninety-one a season and I cannot earn that — I tried it all last year and it took me from a hundred and fifty-five ducats down to seven, and an old man with seven ducats cannot buy medicine the week the fever comes. That is not thrift, it is the arithmetic that keeps me alive. So: plain bread most days, and three good meals bought and set aside for the weeks I feel it coming. Meat as medicine, not as diet. You eat properly every day regardless — that is not part of the bargain and never was. And both candles are lit: San Zaccaria first, then San Giacomo. Twenty-first spring and thirty-second. Sixty years old, and thirty-two Aprils, and not one of them missed.

talk.say: No. And you have made one mistake, Piero, and it is a fatal one: my mother is alive. Agnese Dandolo is sitting in her chair in Castello this morning. You have come to a man with a story about a promise made by a woman you could have walked across the city and asked — and you did not ask her, because you knew what she would say. So let us do it properly. Come with me. Now, today. We will go to her together and you will put it to her face: that in 1353 she promised the north field by San Zaccaria to Piero Dandolo for fifty-four ducats. I will stand silent while you ask. Whatever she says, I will abide by. You will not come, of course. Because here is what my mother actually said to me, in the spring of 1345, holding my hand: that my grandfather swore an oath that no man of the Ferrer would ever have that field, and she made me swear it after him. A woman who guards a piece of ground with two generations of oaths does not quietly sell it eight years later to a moneylender for fifty-four ducats and never mention it to her only son. And I know you, Piero. Winter of 1361, the notary's office — you a moneylender, me refusing you before you had opened your mouth, and I made the notary hear me say that there is no lien on my warehouse and never will be. You have known since that day that I cannot be got at through debt, so now you come at me through my mother's memory instead, and you have waited until she is old and I am sixty. Bring the paper. Her mark, a notary's entry, one living witness. Bring it and I will honour it to the letter, because if my mother truly gave her word then her word is mine and I will hand you the field and thank you for holding me to it. You cannot bring it. And whoever is standing behind you — because a moneylender does not want a field, he wants what he can sell it to a Ferrer for — you may tell them the same thing I told Beatrice Ferrer in 1355 when she offered thirty-seven, a fifth above its worth: there is no number. Not fifty-four. Not five hundred and forty. Now get out of my way, I have rope to make.

Mother, sit up and listen, because this one is worth telling. A man came to me on the Rialto this morning — Piero Dandolo, the moneylender, our own name, the one I refused in the notary's office in '61 before he could open his mouth. He says YOU promised him the north field in 1353 for fifty-four ducats. I told him you were alive and in this house and invited him to come and put it to your face, and that I would abide by whatever you answered. He did not come. Of course he did not. Thirty-three years ago you took my hand and told me about grandfather's oath, and I wrote it down that same afternoon and I have never once needed to guess since. They keep coming for that field, mother — Beatrice Ferrer with thirty-seven in '55, and now this. They will come again after you are gone and after I am gone, and that is exactly why it is written into the will in plain words and read aloud. No Ferrer, and no man buying for a Ferrer, and no number.

talk.say: Nothing in the box, mother. Nothing at all — first time since I was twenty-two. Genoa has the lagoon blockaded, everything costs double, and six ducats a week does not stretch the way it did. So let me say the two things out loud, in this room, while I am hungry and clear-headed, because a hungry man makes his worst decisions quietly. I will not borrow. Not from Piero Dandolo who came here with a lie about you in July, not from any smiling man on the Rialto, not for bread. Thirty-six years I have owed nobody and I am not selling that at sixty for a season's comfort. And I will not sell the warehouse. It stands at five hundred and ten this morning, more than I paid, and there is not a man in Venice who would blame an old ropemaker for taking it. I would blame me. I put six years of my youth into that door and it is the one thing I finished, and a man who sells the thing he finished the first winter it gets hard has finished nothing. We eat plain, I work eleven weeks at sixty years old, and the war ends the way every war ends. And you eat first — that is not a kindness, it is the arrangement, and it has been the arrangement since 1340.

Father, my mother says you asked after me again and I have nothing to bring you this time — the box is empty and Genoa is in the lagoon. But the will stands as it was written: both candles endowed, at San Giacomo and at San Zaccaria, the warehouse to Caterina Ziani and then to my sister's children, and the field never to a Ferrer. I have not touched it and I will not. If I die this winter it all holds without me.

talk.say: Caterina. I am going to ask you for something, and in thirty-eight years I have never asked you for anything except to marry me, so you will know what it costs me to open my mouth. I have two ducats and I have not eaten properly in a season. Genoa has the lagoon shut, everything is double, and six ducats a week does not feed a man any more. I am sixty and my health is going. Now hear the shape of the asking, because the shape matters more to me than the bread. I am NOT asking you for a loan. Do not offer me one; if you put money in my hand I will hand it back the way I handed back Gritti's eighteen and Ferrer's twenty-two, and we will both feel worse. I have owed no man a coin since 1342 and I intend to die that way in whatever year it comes. What I am asking is this: you keep an inn. Feed me. Sit me at your table like anyone else who comes in out of the cold, and let me eat, and let it be a thing given and not a thing lent, with no paper and no account and nothing owed either way — because that is exactly what I offered you in the plague of '48 when your house was full of strangers off the boats and I told you the room was yours whether you ever married me or not. You did not need it then. I need it now. And if you would rather not, say so plainly and I will not think one degree less of you, and I will be on this bridge in the spring as I have been every spring since 1340.

Lucia — sister — I am in trouble and I am telling you rather than being proud about it, which I know is not like me. Two ducats, nothing in the house, hunger the worst it has ever been, and mother to keep. I want no loan and I will take no loan; do not offer me one and do not let your husband offer me one. Bread, if you have any to spare. That is all. And I will say the other half, because it is only fair: for thirty years I sent you word that if you were ever short you should come to Castello and I would pay and take no repayment. I meant it every time and you never once came. I am coming now.

Mother, you eat first this winter and every day of it, and I do not want to hear one word about it. I am at the Arsenale twelve weeks and I have gone to Lucia and to Caterina for bread — asked, not borrowed, and I made the difference very clear to both of them. Thirty-six years without a debt does not end because I am hungry.

talk.say: Mother. I am not well. Nine, I think, if anyone were counting, and I have been counting all my life. So let me get the important thing said while the words are still orderly. Both candles are lit. I went this morning — San Zaccaria first, as always, because that is the newer promise and the newer one is the one that would slip; then across the water to San Giacomo. Twenty-second spring and thirty-third. I had to stop and sit down four times on the way and a fishwife I have never spoken to helped me up the steps, and I got there, and they are burning now. Thirty-three Aprils and not one of them missing — not the plague year, not the year I had eighteen ducats, not this one. And when I go, they do not stop: they are endowed at the notary, both of them, paid for out of the estate, so there will be a candle at San Giacomo and a candle at San Zaccaria for Agnese Dandolo every feast of San Marco after there is no Dandolo left to carry them. You asked me for two things in your whole life. You have had them, and you will go on having them. And the rest holds too: the warehouse is unsold and unmortgaged and there is no lien on it, I owe no living man one coin and have not since 1342, and no Ferrer has the field. They came for it four times and not one of them got a number out of me.

Caterina. If this is the last time — and it may be, I am not going to be coy about it at sixty-one with my hands shaking. Thirty-nine years. Seven proposals, one formal suit to your house, and one answer I never got, and I want to say plainly that I never once held that against you and I do not now. You owed me nothing. That was rather the point of it. The warehouse is yours if you outlive me; it is written, Nicolò has read it, there is no lien and no condition and no claim on your inn. Take it or give it to the Ziani, I do not mind which. And if you go before me I will light a third candle for you every April beside my mother's two, at whichever church you would have named. I did not get the thing I wanted. I got to be somebody who could be relied upon for forty years, and I would not trade that back.

Lucia — if it goes badly this spring: mother is not to be left in that house alone, and the will is lodged and needs nothing doing. Both candles are paid for out of the estate. And tell your boys the one thing worth inheriting from me: no Ferrer ever gets the north field, and nobody in this family ever borrows.
